comments.author: mysteriouspants
comments.text:
once models are cheaper than tools


Why wouldn’t a tool’s execution get cheaper on a similar curve to inference costs?

comments.author: tuxes
comments.text:
The author gives an example of using jgrep
rather than grep.

If I wanted to search a corpus of text for references to sphynx cats, I (or an LLM) could write a regex to search that corpus with grep.

But if I want it to also catch references like "sphinx cats", "them bald cats", or "那种没有毛的猫的品种", then I'm suddenly less confident in this regex.

Maybe I could search the corpus with a tool that uses a parser? Even if I can get it right, that's a lot of parsing! And it's spending as much compute parsing a book about breeds of cats as it as it is books about maths.

Or I could use jgrep, and it's efficiency in part comes from knowing that it needn't focus too hard in documents that are very unlikely to have references to sphynx cats, like physics papers, or lobster.rs comments.

Of course, it'll miss some, but maybe that's okay for the usecase (and maybe it'll miss fewer than the regex or the parser, and spend less compute and energy too).

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
Open weight models can be self-hosted on your own hardware, with your own electricity, and you can calculate your own unsubsidised price per token.

This used to be less meaningful when the frontier closed labs were far ahead of toy open models, but this year we've got large open weight models that are competitive with the best closed models from only a few months ago.

comments.author: andrewballinger
comments.text: Of course it is, at least in the same way your laptop is heavily subsidized by IBM and Casio approximately 50 years ago.

comments.author: mtset
comments.text: This isn't what "subsidized" means. I think we can make some useful analysis about how much inference actually costs some providers, but I don't think it's unreasonable to say that we have very little idea how much inference costs OpenAI and Anthropic. It's entirely possible that they are asking customers for less than it costs them to serve those customers; indeed, since their goal is literally displacing all human knowledge workers, as they have stated, it would be kind of irrational not to do this.

comments.author: andrewballinger
comments.text:
"Computing courses got started in universities largely because IBM donated about 100 ‘free’ computers during the 1950s, with the stipulation that computer courses must be taught. This strategy made it possible for computing to get a foot in the academic door." - Donald Knuth

Businesses frequently do things and operate at a loss in order to enter marketplaces and attract investment to R&D, the advantage to going and reading about IBM and Casio in particular is because they offer two different, extremely relevant, case studies which are very easy to track to the modern day.

IBM ultimately did grab a significant slice of the computing market in the 80s and 90s. Read about it!

The actual accounting for a company like Open AI who has a major investor in Microsoft, a cloud services operator, which has unbooked (wasted) compute, is complex...

It also doesn't say anything about investment banking 'hyperscaler' lunacy, which thank gods a lot of investors are pulling back on... and really doesn't have anything to do directly with who is funding the development of this technology and what's going to happen in the next 5/10/20 years... personally I think the majority of academic subsidy ends up working out for everyone involved.

comments.author: timthelion
comments.text: This isn't about marketing claims, this is just basic hardware benchmarking. The inference hardware is getting more efficient per watt. This is not surprising. Everything is getting more efficient per watt over time.

comments.author: gulbanana
comments.text: Since this post was written, there have actually been some more price-efficiency improvements from the U.S. LLM companies. New versions of Claude Opus, GPT Luna and GPT Sol have been reached, each (according to claimed benchmarks) cheaper and more capable than the previous versions of those models. For now, the trend continues.
